Hi Samira — thanks for the clear list. We prepared a compact but runnable response set and attached three artifacts: stress-resilience-matrix.csv (CSV you can ingest), test-harness-runbook.pdf (step-by-step to reproduce our lab runs), and a small sample-run JSONL with parsed telemetry. High-level answers below; the runbook has scripts, k6 profiles, and expected machine specs.

Summary (short):
- Methodology: we recommend three canonical load shapes (steady-state, diurnal-with-burst, and sudden-spike). For each shape run: 30 min warmup, 60 min steady period, and an accelerated saturation sweep (linear concurrency ramp to 120% of target capacity over 10 min).
- Metrics reported: time-to-first-token (TTFT), time-to-last-token (TTLT), per-request token-count, request/second (RPS), tokens/sec (TPS), GPU utilization, and end-to-end P50/P95/P99 for both TTFT and TTLT. We include stream-first and stream-complete percentiles.
- Representative numbers (lab, Dedicated pool, Llama2-13B-Int8, sequence 64 tokens request + 256 tokens response):
  - Steady throughput (no batching, single-request execution): sustained 220 RPS (approx 56k tokens/sec output) at P50 TTFT ~ 28 ms, P95 TTFT ~ 95 ms, P99 TTFT ~ 180 ms. TTLT P50 ~ 60 ms, P95 ~ 210 ms, P99 ~ 420 ms.
  - With batching enabled (continuous batching, batch size ~ 8): throughput increases ~2.8x, sustained ~620 RPS, but P50 TTFT increases by ~18-30ms depending on arrival pattern.
- Quantization effects: int8 quantization reduces per-token compute by ~35-45% vs float16 in our runs; expect lower throughput in float16 by that factor. Quantization sometimes increases P99 variance slightly for long-context models; include that in runbook.
- KV/prefix caching: our KV-cache provides dramatic improvements for repeated-prefix workloads — observed 40-70% reduction in compute on subsequent completions after a cache hit; include cache-miss vs cache-hit curves in the CSV. Cache warming in a steady workload typically converges within ~5–12 minutes depending on request diversity.
- Saturation behavior: latency percentiles rise slowly up to ~65–70% GPU utilization, after which p95 and p99 climb non-linearly. At 85–95% sustained utilization expect p99 to degrade by 2–4x relative to baseline; beyond that tail latencies can spike and error rates (queue drops) may appear. We recommend SLOs keep steady-state at <= 70% utilization with autoscaling headroom to 90% for short bursts.
- Graceful degradation: runtime supports automatic fallback to lower-cost model variants (Llama2-7B-Int8) and soft-throttling (queue-based shedding) with token-limited responses. We also support route-level fallback: if primary Dedicated pool is saturated, route traffic to lower-cost region or hosted pool depending on policy.

Test harness & reproducibility:
- We provide k6 + custom gRPC/HTTP replayer samples in the runbook. Profiles: steady.json (constant RPS), diurnal.json (sinusoidal load), spike.json (sudden 5x burst for 5 minutes), and long-tail.json (Pareto inter-arrival to simulate production).
- Measurement instrumentation: we record request scope tracing ids, client-to-proxy latency, proxy-to-inference latency, and GPU-level metrics. We correlate traces to surface TTFT and TTLT. All sample outputs are in the attached sample-run-2027-07-21.jsonl.

Deliverables we can provide for RFP:
- Completed stress-resilience matrix CSV (attached)
- Test-harness-runbook PDF (attached), contains exact scripts and a small Docker environment to run locally
- Sample telemetry JSONL (attached)
- Optional: we can run a co-validated lab test with Aurora engineers for an agreed scope (we'd schedule dedicated capacity).

Next steps: if you want, we can run a short validation run targeting the Llama2-13B-Int8 profile in your environment (we provide test VMs and harness); this usually takes 2–3 business days to coordinate.

Hi Samira — quick clarifications inline and a short p99 table attached below for your slide.

Measurement boundaries: we measure TTFT and TTLT end-to-end from the client-side test harness (post-TLS handshake). That includes tokenization and request marshalling on the client but does not include one-time TLS session establishment (i.e., we time after the TLS session is up). For reproducible lab runs we recommend re-using TLS sessions or priming connections for the warmup period.

Streaming: we report both TTFB/TTFT (time-to-first-token) and TTLT. For streaming-heavy workloads we recommend using TTFT as the primary interactive SLO and TTLT for completion SLAs. Our sample-run contains both metrics per request.

Private deployments and encryption: KMS/HSM calls for key unwrap add a small one-time cost on model start (cold start) ~5–18ms depending on provider; per-request encryption overhead on TLS is negligible (2–6ms). If you instrument with a proxy in your VPC, model the network RTT and jitter separately; we include a network emulation section in the runbook (tc/netem profiles).

Small p99 guidance (example measured, Llama2-13B-Int8, 64/256 request/response, single busy Dedicated pool):
- 60% GPU util: p99 TTFT = 190 ms
- 70% GPU util: p99 TTFT = 220 ms
- 80% GPU util: p99 TTFT = 480 ms
- 90% GPU util: p99 TTFT = 920 ms
- 95% GPU util: p99 TTFT = 1.9 s (on long sustained runs you may also see queue drops)

Notes: those numbers are lab measurements and will vary with hardware generation (A100 vs H100), model size, sequence length, and batching policy. The CSV includes the corresponding TTLT numbers too.

If helpful I can boil this into a single-slide PDF for your SRE deck — would you like that?

Best,
Naomi
